Choosing the goal: what to send a servo so the joint lands where you want

One general formula for the goal sent to a servo. Every controller I built, from a plain look-ahead to MPC, is that formula with some terms set to zero.

Whole board

Here is an SO-101 arm drawing with a pen. Every command interval (33 ms at 30 Hz), the computer sends each of the five servos one number, the goal angle. That number is the only thing we control, and this article is about what it should be.

The obvious choice is the angle you want the joint at. A baseline modeled on LeRobot's behavior does roughly that, and over a 120 s drawing on the real arm it misses by 22.5 mrad RMS across the five joints. A planner that chooses the goal with care brings the same arm, on the same drawing, to 6.0 mrad. (The planner ran at 60 Hz and the baseline at 30 Hz, so this comparison changes both the controller and the command rate.) I love gaps like this one, because the error traces back to a few physical effects, each effect has its own fix, and once you can tell them apart the controller more or less writes itself. Part 1 built the servo model and Part 2 showed how to read the joint finer than the encoder. Let's start with the servo.

The servo pushes only when the goal is somewhere else

The servo reads its own angle q, compares it with the goal, and makes torque in proportion to the difference: torque = kp(goal − q). Put the goal exactly where the joint is and you get zero torque. The servo is a spring, and the goal is where we pin its far end.

Now hold the arm out with a 150 g tool in the gripper. The shoulder-lift joint needs 0.378 N·m to keep that tool up, and its servo stiffness is kp = 13.64 N·m/rad. The servo can only make 0.378 N·m with a gap of 0.378 / 13.64 = 27.7 mrad. So if we send goal = target, the joint sags until that gap opens, then sits 27.7 mrad low, perfectly still, with exactly the torque it needs. The fix is to put the goal 27.7 mrad above the target. The same logic covers every force on the joint: gravity, the inertia of speeding up and slowing down, damping, friction. The servo has to produce each of them, so each one needs its own goal offset, equal to that force divided by kp. From here on, the target q* is where we want the joint, and the goal is the number we send.

The goal is a sum, one term per error

If we knew the arm perfectly, the goal would be

goal(t) = q*(t+D) + (Mq̈* + G + dq̇* + f sign(q̇*) + Cq̇*) / kp

The first term looks ahead by the servo's dead time D. The rest turn the forces from inertia M, gravity G, damping d, friction f and coupling between joints C into goal offsets. We never know these exactly, so every controller in this article uses estimates (the hats) and adds terms that patch what the estimates miss. We just worked out the offset for holding the tool still. What happens when we move it? The servo responds late, accelerating the tool takes extra torque, and we might not even know how heavy it is. We'll handle those problems one at a time; the equation below shows where each correction will go, and the board labels every term. Each controller in the lab switches some terms on and leaves the rest at zero. Click through them:

goal = q*(t + T) + (M̂q̈* + Ĉq̇* + Ĝ(q*) + d̂q̇* + f̂ sign(q̇*)) / kp + τ̂network / kp + ŵ + KPe + KI∫e dt + uk

Every controller in the lab

piinv + KP = 0.2, KI = 2 s⁻¹

Aim where the target will be

Start with time. A goal sent now doesn't move the joint now. The servo waits out a dead time, then responds with a lag of about d/kp, and each command is held for a whole interval on top of that. On the real arm the joint trails the target by 87 to 105 ms. Feedback can't fix this. It sees the error only after the joint has missed, and its correction then waits out the same dead time, so by the time it lands the target has moved on. The cure is to aim ahead.

The lead controller does the cheapest version and sends the target one interval early, about 33 ms at 30 Hz. The inv controller also inverts the lag:

goal(t) = q*(t + 33 ms) + 0.106 s · q̇*(t) + 0.0023 s² · q̈*(t)

The velocity term pays for the lag and the acceleration term for inertia. We fitted that 0.0023 s² from a step response rather than from link masses, so it can soak up other acceleration effects too, and per-joint fitted files replace these shared constants. Both derivatives come from the planned path, so nothing differentiates noisy encoder readings. On a signature-tracing path on the real arm at 30 Hz, RMS goes from 28.3 mrad with direct to 23.7 with lead to 13.4 with inv. Aiming ahead removed about half the error.

inv still has no gravity term, so an outstretched arm keeps sagging. Two variants add it. sag fits sines and cosines of the link angles to steady holds, and grav takes the gravity torque at the target pose from a MuJoCo model and divides it by kp. Fitting from holds has a trap: in the October 3 logs, friction hid the pose dependence, and the fit came out as a nearly constant offset per joint.

The timing plot from the experiments

Feedback for the force nobody modeled

We can model the arm's own gravity. The 150 g tool might be a surprise, and this is where feedback earns its place. Add an outer loop that pushes the goal by four times the measured error e = q* − q̂, so goal = q* + 4e, and guess the leftover sag before reading on.

With goal = q* + 4e and the unknown 0.378 N·m load, where does the joint settle?

  1. 27.7 mrad low
  2. 6.9 mrad low
  3. 5.5 mrad low
  4. on target
Answer

5.5 mrad low. The servo's own spring adds to the outer loop; the next paragraph works it out.

The servo already makes torque from the gap, and now the gap is (q* − q) + 4e = 5e. So the effective stiffness is (1 + 4) × 13.64 = 68.2 N·m/rad, and the error under the unknown 0.378 N·m is 0.378 / 68.2 ≈ 5.5 mrad, against 27.7 with no feedback. (This static calculation leaves out friction and integral action.) The tempting answer, 27.7 / 4 = 6.9 mrad, forgets that the servo's own spring was already pulling.

So why not set the gain to 100? An encoder tick is about 1.53 mrad, so at gain 100 one noisy tick throws the goal 153 mrad. Dead time makes it worse. Within one 33 ms interval the servo covers only about 0.15 of a goal change, so the loop keeps correcting errors that are already being fixed. Even the modest Classical gains of 4 and 10, run with 33 ms of hardware-like dead time in the shake simulation below, kept the torque saturated about 95% of the time. Feedback works best as a small correction on top of a model: on a stiff simulated robot, outer PID alone saturated on 10.9% of steps, and the same feedback on top of the model offset saturated on 0%.

The hardware loop is therefore gentle: goal = goalinv + 0.2e + 2 s⁻¹ ∫e dt, with both terms limited. The integral keeps growing while any steady error remains, so it ends up holding exactly the missing goal offset. In other words, it is a disturbance estimator that assumes the disturbance never changes. Raise the gains below and watch both the load step at 3 s and the point where the delayed loop starts to ring.

Servo playground: one joint tracks a 0.1 rad sine with inv feedforward plus your outer gains. A 0.378 N·m load arrives at 3 s.

An illustrative toy model: kp = 13.64 N·m/rad, 33 ms dead time, 30 Hz commands and 1.53 mrad encoder ticks.

The two springs, drawn

Shake the tool: what a constant can't fix

Let's make the tool move. In MuJoCo we hold the SO-101 forward with the 150 g load, 33 ms of dead time and a 30 Hz loop, then wiggle one joint by 0.1 rad at 1 Hz: the shoulder lift, which fights gravity, or the shoulder pan, which swings horizontally and doesn't.

direct on the vertical axis misses by 87.9 mrad RMS with a mean error of 50 mrad, which is the sag. Integral feedback drives that mean to zero, yet the RMS only drops to 76.5. On the horizontal axis there's no sag to remove, and the integral changes nothing (65.5 to 66.1). What's left is inertia. Swinging the link and tool back and forth takes a force that flips sign every half cycle, and an integrator slowly learning a constant can never catch it. Adding inv's timing and acceleration terms cuts the error to 21.8 and 11.0. We can go further by asking MuJoCo how much torque the arm will need along the upcoming path, then adding the corresponding goal offsets before the joint falls behind. That brings RMS error to 6.0 mrad vertically and 1.8 horizontally, even without telling the model about the tool. Include the tool's mass and both fall to 0.8 mrad. Changing demand needs anticipation, and steady demand needs an estimate. Two limits apply here: the torque never saturated, so braking early under a torque limit is untested, and the preview is plain feedforward, so this test says nothing about MPC.

Shake test traces and RMS

Inside one 33 ms command

Even with good force models, some error remains. The Classical controller (one-interval preview, feedforward for inertia, gravity, damping and friction, plus KP = 4 and KI = 10) does what we have done so far: it solves kp(goal − q) = τ for the torque it wants at the target instant. Give Classical and an Exact controller the true parameters of six simulated robots, tune each one's gains, and Classical averages 1.312 mrad against 0.385, a 3.4× gap. Where does it come from?

Both controllers know the true parameters. What costs Classical the factor of 3.4?

  1. its friction law
  2. small parameter errors
  3. no derivative feedback
  4. the goal is held for 33 ms while the joint moves
Answer

The held command, explained next.

The goal is held for 33 ms while q keeps moving, so the gap, and with it the torque, changes during the interval. In an illustrative interval at 0.84 rad/s, the modeled torque falls from 1.27 to 0.886 N·m while Classical assumes 0.886 the whole time. One-factor-at-a-time tests in MuJoCo pointed at this hold, ahead of the friction law, parameter errors and missing derivative feedback. The same Classical rule scores 4.13 mrad at 30 Hz and 0.91 at 240 Hz, where each held command is eight times shorter.

So treat the interval as an interval. Fitted simulates the servo through eight substeps and uses Newton's method to find the goal whose end state minimizes

J = |q1 − rk+1|² + (0.5Δt)² |v1 − ṙk+1|²

where q1 and v1 are the angle and speed at the end of the interval and r is the target. The speed term is there because arriving at the right angle too fast means overshooting right after. The factor (0.5Δt)² turns speed error into position error: at 33 ms, 0.1 rad/s counts like about 1.7 mrad. Why 0.5? We tried several weights for the speed error, and this one gave the lowest tracking error. Fitted runs with KP = 0 and KI = 3, and Exact is the same controller handed the true supply, damping, friction and payload parameters (it still sees rounded encoder readings).

The torque inside one interval

Dead band and ticks: where the slope goes flat

Real servos ignore small gaps, and the goal can only be a whole encoder tick. Both break the smooth picture. Take a toy joint with a ±10 mrad dead band, sitting at 100 mrad with the target at 115. Any goal from 90 to 110 makes zero torque, so the joint stays put and the error stays at 15 mrad. Above 110 the joint follows the goal minus 10, so the best goal is 125. Plot the cost against the goal and you get a flat plateau right where a search would naturally start. A gradient method standing on it sees slope zero and has no idea which way to go. A search over whole ticks never needed a slope, so that's what the planners do.

The band also makes small corrections expensive. With the joint at 100, the last goal at 110 and the target dropping to 99, moving down a single mrad means dropping the goal below 90, a 20 mrad reversal. Send 88, the joint lands at 98, and coming back up needs a goal above 108, another 20 mrad jump. An optimizer allowed to do this freely chatters at up to 17 reversals per second. So we make the planner a little stubborn. It keeps the current goal unless changing it would improve the predicted error by at least half a tick. Reversing direction takes more: at least 1.5 ticks of improvement (about 2.3 mrad), with at least 0.2 s since the last reversal. Reversals that follow the target's own motion are always allowed. Chatter falls to at most 1.8 per second, at the price of 0.4 to 1.0 mrad of extra hold error, and static errors under about 1.5 ticks can stay.

The dead-band cost plot

Plan a quarter second, send one goal

Put the pieces together and you get model predictive control (MPC). At every interval the planner reads the rounded encoder, previews the next 0.25 s of target, simulates candidate goal sequences through a fitted servo model, picks the cheapest, and sends only its first goal. At the next reading it throws the rest away and plans again. The 0.25 s is about one dead time plus two servo lags, long enough to see what this goal does. It is also why the lab MPC needs no explicit speed term: an overshoot shows up inside its own horizon.

The per-joint model holds delay, lag, dead band, stiffness and pose sag, with sag stored as radians of steady goal offset. A slow disturbance estimate moves Δt/(0.3 s) of the way toward any unexplained error at each interval. Here the sum from earlier stops being a literal sum: dead band, integer ticks, held commands and torque limits enter through simulation and the choice between candidates.

We could choose every goal in the next quarter second independently. Or we could choose just one destination and use a fixed rule to fill in the goals on the way there.

Which gives the planner fewer choices to search?

  1. every goal in the 0.25 s plan chosen independently
  2. one whole-tick destination per joint, with a fixed fill-in rule
Answer

One integer-tick destination per joint. A fixed rule fills in the goals on the way there.

That smaller search is solve: one whole-tick destination per joint. mpc takes the bigger one and chooses every goal on its own: 8 at 30 Hz, 15 at 60 Hz, 25 at 100 Hz. Its cost is the mean squared tracking error, plus a small penalty for changing commands more than inv would and a smaller one for straying from inv. More freedom means more plateaus to get stuck on, so how should it start?

The cost is flat across the dead band. How should mpc start its search?

  1. from inv, following the gradient
  2. score offsets that span the band, then refine the best
  3. shrink the dead band in the model
  4. raise the feedback gain
Answer

Score candidates that span the band, then refine. Details next.

It scores 50 candidates (49 constant offsets added to inv, spanning the band, plus the previous plan shifted by one interval), keeps the best, and takes two Gauss-Newton steps from there. The candidates drop the search somewhere with a usable slope. Try both on the toy:

Plan compare: the toy dead band from above. Start at goal 100, try a gradient step, then a whole-tick search, and switch between a solve-style and an mpc-style plan over 0.25 s.

Why a small per-joint model and not the full MuJoCo arm? Time. A 0.25 s MuJoCo rollout takes about 0.75 ms on a Mac, and a 100 Hz planner has about 2 ms per interval for dozens of candidates. Coupling between joints makes it worse, since the candidates become combinations of five joint goals instead of five separate searches. Physical detail also buys less than you'd hope when nobody measured this arm's masses: on held-out arm logs, a fitted Genesis model predicted the elbow with 13.5 mrad of error against 16.1 for the small servo model. We picked the model by prediction accuracy per millisecond.

Where inverse kinematics fits

A tool like Mink turns a gripper pose into joint angles through geometry, with no servo dynamics and no look-ahead in time. solve works downstream of that: it takes joint targets that are already decided and picks servo commands over time.

Estimate the load as it changes

The integral assumed the missing force is constant. A Kalman filter, the estimator from Part 2, can do better. adapt predicts each joint's angle with the fixed model, compares the prediction with the encoder, and splits the mismatch into a fast load, a slow sag and friction. Another option is to update the model itself. rls uses the last two positions and goals to keep fitting a small linear model of the joint, gradually giving older data less weight. This update is called recursive least squares. It then works backward through the updated model to choose the next goal. mpca puts the adapt estimate inside MPC in place of the slow one. In a simulated load step at 30 Hz, mpca reaches 2.5 mrad against 3.7 for mpc. On the real arm, over one 120 s motion at 60 Hz with fitted arm constants, shoulder-lift RMS is 10.3 mrad for mpca against 87.6 for direct, whose 70 mrad mean error is mostly sag at extended poses.

The last term, uk, handles errors that come back at the same step of the same motion every run. ilc learns it on top of inv, ilcmpc on top of planning, and a network can learn the torque-offset term itself. Part 4 develops these approaches and combines physics with a network that learns only the torque correction the physics misses.

What the scores say

First the clean test. In simulation the true parameters are known, so we can run 96 held-out paths of 6 s each, none used for tuning, with every controller fed the same rounded encoder readings. Rank four of them before you look at the board:

Rank these four from worst to best on the 96 held-out paths. Click them in order.

  1. network
  2. baseline
  3. Fitted
  4. Classical
Answer

Worst to best: baseline 37.2, Classical 1.117, network 0.446, Fitted 0.398 mrad RMS.

The baseline scores 37.2 mrad and Classical 1.117. The network gets to 0.446, and Fitted reaches 0.398 after 24 s of identification data, the same as Exact. Rounding a single encoder reading already costs 0.443 mrad RMS, so the best controllers track finer than one reading can resolve (Part 2 explains how).

The real arm is messier. Over the full 120 s cat drawing at 60 Hz, pi scores 8.4 mrad, solve 6.2 and mpc 6.0. Per joint, planning helps the pan, lift, elbow and roll and hurts the wrist flex (7.0 for pi, 8.7 and 8.6 for the planners). In the fastest speed bin pi wins outright, 11.7 against 14.2 and 13.4. The planners hit a step limit on 1 to 3% of intervals, a possible cause that nobody has verified yet. Each controller ran once.

Choose the term by the error

When the arm misses, name the error before you touch a gain. The matrix maps each controller to the errors it removes. It comes from the controller designs and simulation, and on hardware only pi has been checked, on one motion.

● removes the error, ◐ removes part of it.

Where these ideas come from

None of this is new. Inverse-dynamics feedforward plus feedback is computed-torque control, from the 1980s (1981 on the timeline). Estimating an unknown load online is adaptive control: Slotine and Li (1987) estimated mass parameters online with a stability proof, using the fact that robot dynamics are linear in those parameters. MPC with a Kalman-estimated disturbance is offset-free MPC (1990s and 2000s), so mpca is an established classical design. uk is iterative learning control (Arimoto, 1984), and the Kalman filter dates to about 1960. The lab controllers borrow these ideas; nobody proved that each implementation meets the original theory.

Once the error is named, spend your effort on the model inside the controller, and pick that model by how well it predicts the joint within the computation you can afford each interval.
